newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood rockets Kabul airport, closes in on capital.
newsitem.headline: Masood rockets Kabul airport, closes in on capital.

text.p: Ousted Afghan military chief Ahmad Shah Masood sent rockets slamming into Kabul airport on Sunday, signalling to his fundamentalist foes that his forces are closing in on the capital.

Reuter correspondent Kurt Schork, travelling with Masood's front line troops, reported that Masood's men took the village of Hussein Kot on Sunday morning, putting them just 20 km (12 miles) from the city.
That left Masood with a 15 km (eight-mile) stretch of the main road leading from the north across a lightly-populated dusty plain before his men reached the entrance to the Kabul valley.
"God willing, we will be in Kabul today or tomorrow," Masood commander Gul Haider said in Hussein Kot, which radicals of the Taleban militia were peppering with mortar, artillery and rocket fire.

Masood spokesman Mirabuddin Astana told reporters the Uzbek forces of northern Uzbek warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum, which joined Masood last week, were pushing down a parallel road to Kabul and were about 30 km (18 miles) from the city.
About two hours later a barrage of rockets exploded around Kabul airport where the fundamentalist Moslem militia, which took the capital three weeks ago, base part of their air force.
At least seven rockets landed within the perimeter of the sprawling airport and aircraft, civilian and military, immediately took off.
Most of the rockets landed at the military end of the airport and some of the aircraft moved to the other side. Others flew off, but it was not clear where they were going.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage and the airport was tense, but calm.

The city, which has been ravaged by factional fighting over the past four years, took the rocket barrage in its stride, but the explosions were a stark reminder of just how close is yet another battle for control of the capital.
Taleban spokesmen declined to talk to reporters about what their ultra-conservative movement would do, but they have previously spurned warnings from Masood to quit the city or face battle.
They have said the Taleban have enough men to defend Kabul, but their fighters on the main road north showed signs of alarm as Masood's men inched ever nearer the capital.
At the top of the pass leading into Kabul on Sunday morning, a Taleban guard pointed his gun at a Taleban pickup truck and told the driver to get back to the fighting.
The vehicle was allowed to drive into the city only after pointing to a wounded fighter in the back.
Two weeks ago, Masood's mainly Tajik fighters were driven back into their Panjsher Valley stronghold some 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul, but hit back with some stunning counter-attacks.
His latest breakthrough came on Friday when, with the backing of Dostum's artillery, he took Bagram airbase some 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.
Since then he has pushed another 25 km (12 miles) south along the main road. Some of the few people allowed to travel to Kabul from the area say there have been many civilian casualties.
But people just south of the front lines on Sunday morning were cheering on Masood, accusing Taleban fighters of beating his suspected supporters and forcing villagers to cook food for them.
"We are absolutely fed up with the Taleban. If Masood would give us some help, we would fight them," said a grey-bearded farmer whose family was ready to flee the area.
Scores of refugees were already walking down the road to Kabul, carrying what they could and driving donkeys laden with possessions.
